title: St. John's Wort and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink?
excerpt: Can you drink while taking St. John's wort? How the herb changes your liver's drug-clearing enzymes, why alcohol undermines its mood benefit, and which medicine combinations are genuinely risky.
metaDescription: Can you drink on St. John's wort? How it changes liver enzymes, why alcohol works against its mood benefit, and which drug combinations are actually risky.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** treat St. John's wort as a medicine with serious interactions, not a harmless herb. It speeds up the liver enzymes (mainly CYP3A4) and drug pumps that clear dozens of prescription drugs, so birth control, blood thinners, heart, HIV, transplant, and anti-anxiety medicines can quietly stop working. It also raises serotonin, so combining it with antidepressants, triptans, tramadol, or the cough suppressant dextromethorphan can cause serotonin syndrome, which can be life-threatening. Alcohol itself doesn't react with the herb in a well-documented way, but it makes many of those same medicines riskier and works against the low mood people take the herb for. If you take St. John's wort, whether you drink at all is a question for your doctor or pharmacist, especially if you take anything else.

**The quick rules:** Before drinking on St. John's wort, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether alcohol is okay for you, and how much. Don't combine it with prescription antidepressants, migraine triptans, tramadol, or other serotonin-boosting drugs unless a doctor has approved it. Tell your doctor and pharmacist you take it, because it can make birth control, blood thinners, heart drugs, anti-anxiety medicines, HIV drugs, and transplant drugs less effective. If you've been drinking heavily to cope with low mood, raise that with a doctor directly rather than treating it with an herb.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and official guidance about St. John's wort. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and full medication list. **Talk to your doctor before combining St. John's wort with alcohol if** you take any prescription medicine, use hormonal birth control, have been diagnosed with depression or bipolar disorder, or drink most days. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you notice agitation, confusion, a racing heart, high fever, heavy sweating, muscle twitching or stiffness, or shivering after mixing St. John's wort with another medicine, since these can be signs of serotonin syndrome. If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US) right away.

## What St. John's Wort Is and How It Works

St. John's wort (*Hypericum perforatum*) is a yellow-flowered plant that has been used in European folk medicine for centuries. Today it's one of the best-selling herbal supplements in the world, mostly taken for low mood, mild depression, and sometimes anxiety or menopausal symptoms. In the US it's sold as a dietary supplement, which means it isn't approved by the FDA to treat any condition and products vary in strength. In parts of Europe, standardized extracts have been prescribed for mild to moderate depression.

The plant contains a mix of active compounds. The two that get the most attention are **hyperforin** and **hypericin**. Researchers believe hyperforin is responsible for much of the mood effect, because it appears to slow the reuptake (the recycling) of several brain chemicals at once, including serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. That's a broader effect than most prescription antidepressants, which mainly target serotonin.

The evidence for mood is genuinely mixed. A Cochrane review led by Klaus Linde (2008) pooled dozens of trials and concluded that St. John's wort extracts worked better than placebo for major depression and about as well as standard antidepressants, with fewer side effects. But the results depended heavily on where the trials were done, with German-speaking countries reporting stronger effects than elsewhere. A large US trial published in *JAMA* in 2002 by the Hypericum Depression Trial Study Group found that neither St. John's wort nor the antidepressant sertraline beat placebo for moderately severe major depression. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) describes the overall picture as uncertain, and warns most loudly about its drug interactions.

That second point matters more than the mood debate for anyone thinking about alcohol, so it's where we'll start.

## The Real Interaction: St. John's Wort Revs Up Your Liver's Drug-Clearing Enzymes

The single most important fact about St. John's wort is that it **speeds up the breakdown of many other drugs.** It does this through a switch inside liver and gut cells called the pregnane X receptor (PXR). Hyperforin turns this switch on. Once it's on, your cells make more of certain drug-processing proteins, mainly:

- **CYP3A4**, an enzyme that breaks down roughly half of all prescription drugs
- **CYP2C19** and **CYP2C9**, enzymes that handle drugs like some acid reducers, some anti-seizure drugs, and the blood thinner warfarin
- **P-glycoprotein**, a pump that pushes certain drugs back out of your gut and cells before they can work

Think of it like hiring extra cleaning staff. Drugs that rely on those enzymes get cleared faster, so blood levels drop and the medicine may stop working properly. This effect builds up over about one to two weeks of regular use, and it can take a similar amount of time to wear off after you stop. That's why simply skipping a dose of St. John's wort on the night you drink doesn't reset anything.

### Where alcohol fits in

Here's the nuance most articles skip. Alcohol itself is mostly broken down by a different set of enzymes: **alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH)** in the liver and stomach, plus **CYP2E1**, which picks up more of the work in people who drink heavily. CYP3A4 plays only a minor role. There's no good evidence that St. John's wort meaningfully speeds up or slows down how fast you sober up, or that it raises your blood alcohol level.

So the interaction isn't "St. John's wort plus alcohol makes a toxic chemical." It's three overlapping problems:

1. **Alcohol undermines the mood benefit** you're taking the herb for.
2. **Both can affect the brain and your coordination**, so some people feel more dizzy or drowsy than they expect.
3. **St. John's wort changes your other medicines**, and alcohol often makes those same medicines riskier. Mixing all three is where real danger shows up.

## Problem 1: Alcohol Works Against the Reason You're Taking It

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. That doesn't mean it makes you sad in the moment (the first drink often lifts mood), but over hours and days it pushes the other way. As alcohol wears off, the brain swings into a rebound state that can bring anxiety, irritability, poor sleep, and low mood the next day. Regular drinking is strongly linked with depression, and the relationship runs in both directions: low mood can lead to drinking, and drinking can deepen low mood. Our guide to [alcohol and depression](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-depression) covers that loop in detail, and [is alcohol a depressant?](/never-hungover/is-alcohol-a-depressant) explains what "depressant" actually means.

Alcohol also wrecks sleep quality. It may help you fall asleep, but it fragments the second half of the night and suppresses REM sleep. Poor sleep is one of the strongest drivers of low mood. If you're taking St. John's wort to feel steadier, a few nights of drinking a week can easily cancel out whatever modest benefit it gives you, and then it looks like the herb "isn't working."

This is the same reason doctors usually advise limiting alcohol on prescription antidepressants. It isn't only about a chemical clash. It's that alcohol pulls mood in the opposite direction.

## Problem 2: Dizziness, Drowsiness, and Feeling More Drunk

St. John's wort isn't a strong sedative, and many people feel nothing unusual when they have a glass of wine while taking it. But common side effects of the herb include dizziness, tiredness, dry mouth, upset stomach, and restlessness. Alcohol causes several of the same things. Some product labels advise avoiding alcohol for this reason.

In practice, the combination may leave you:

- More lightheaded or unsteady than usual for the amount you drank
- More tired the next day
- More prone to stomach upset or nausea

Even for an otherwise healthy person who takes no other medicine, the safest approach is to ask your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on St. John's wort, assume alcohol may hit harder than usual, and never drive after drinking.

## Problem 3: The Medication Chain Reaction

This is where St. John's wort and alcohol can turn into a real safety issue. Many people who take St. John's wort also take, or have been prescribed, other medicines. Some of those don't mix with alcohol on their own, and St. John's wort changes how they behave.

### Serotonin syndrome risk

Because St. John's wort raises serotonin activity, combining it with other drugs that do the same can cause **serotonin syndrome**, a potentially dangerous build-up of serotonin. Drugs that raise this risk include:

- **SSRIs and SNRIs** such as sertraline (Zoloft), escitalopram (Lexapro), fluoxetine (Prozac), and venlafaxine
- **Triptans** for migraine, such as sumatriptan
- **Tramadol** and some other painkillers
- **Dextromethorphan**, the cough suppressant in many cold medicines, including some products people reach for after a night out
- **MAO inhibitors**, linezolid, and some other medicines

Alcohol doesn't directly cause serotonin syndrome, but heavy drinking can make it harder to notice early signs, and people who drink to cope with mood are more likely to be combining several mood-related medicines. If you're on any prescription antidepressant, don't add St. John's wort on your own. Our guides on [antidepressants and alcohol](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol), [Zoloft and alcohol](/never-hungover/zoloft-and-alcohol), and [Lexapro and alcohol](/never-hungover/lexapro-and-alcohol) cover those drugs specifically.

### Drugs St. John's wort can make less effective

Because it speeds up CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, St. John's wort can lower blood levels of many medicines. Well-documented examples include:

- **Hormonal birth control** (pills, and likely other hormonal methods). Breakthrough bleeding and unplanned pregnancies have been reported. Use a backup method and talk to your prescriber.
- **Warfarin** and some other blood thinners
- **Digoxin**, a heart rhythm medicine
- **Cyclosporine and tacrolimus**, transplant drugs. Organ rejection has been reported in people who started St. John's wort.
- **Some HIV medicines**, such as indinavir and other protease inhibitors
- **Some cancer drugs**, such as irinotecan
- **Some benzodiazepines** like alprazolam (Xanax), plus some statins and some sleep medicines

### Why alcohol makes this worse

Alcohol adds a few twists on top of those interactions:

- **The anxiety-medicine trap.** If St. John's wort lowers your alprazolam level, the medicine may feel weaker and you might be tempted to take more or to drink to calm down. Alcohol plus benzodiazepines is a genuinely dangerous combination that can slow breathing. See our guide to [anxiety medication and alcohol](/never-hungover/anxiety-medication-and-alcohol).
- **The birth control double hit.** St. John's wort can already make the pill less reliable. Vomiting after heavy drinking can also stop a pill from being absorbed if it happens within a few hours of taking it. Together, that's two separate ways to lose protection in the same weekend.
- **Blood thinners and bleeding.** Heavy drinking can change how warfarin behaves and raise bleeding risk on its own. Adding an herb that also shifts warfarin levels makes the dose harder to keep steady.
- **The morning-after medicine cabinet.** Many cold, flu, and cough products contain dextromethorphan, which adds to the serotonin risk. Check labels before reaching for one while you take St. John's wort.

If you take any prescription medicine at all, the single most useful step is a five-minute conversation with a pharmacist. They can check your full list in a few seconds. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers how supplements and common drugs interact more broadly.

## Can You Drink While Taking St. John's Wort?

For a healthy adult who takes no other medicine, there's no well-documented dangerous reaction between the herb and alcohol itself. But that's a narrow case, the herb's effect on other drugs lasts for weeks, and alcohol undercuts the reason most people take it. Whether you drink, and how much, is worth settling with your doctor or pharmacist. A practical way to think about it:

| Your situation | What it means |
|---|---|
| No other medicines, occasional drinking | Ask your pharmacist first. Watch for extra dizziness and drowsiness, and don't drive. |
| Drinking several times a week or bingeing | Likely undermines any mood benefit. Worth cutting back or talking to a doctor about how you're feeling. |
| Taking an antidepressant, triptan, or tramadol | Don't add St. John's wort without your doctor's approval, regardless of alcohol. |
| Using hormonal birth control | Talk to your prescriber and use a backup method. Heavy drinking and vomiting add another risk. |
| Taking blood thinners, heart, HIV, transplant, or anti-anxiety drugs | Ask your doctor before taking St. John's wort at all. Alcohol adds to the risk with several of these. |
| Diagnosed depression or bipolar disorder | Talk to your doctor. St. John's wort has been linked with triggering mania in some people with bipolar disorder. |

If you notice that you're drinking more to manage your mood, or that your mood is getting worse despite the herb, that's a sign to talk to a doctor rather than adjust the supplement on your own.

## Does St. John's Wort Help With Alcohol Cravings?

You may have seen claims that St. John's wort reduces the urge to drink. This idea comes almost entirely from animal research. Several studies in rats bred to prefer alcohol found that hypericum extracts lowered how much alcohol the animals chose to drink. Researchers have suggested this could relate to the herb's effects on serotonin and dopamine.

But there is no good evidence from human trials that St. John's wort reduces alcohol cravings or helps people drink less. Rat drinking behavior doesn't reliably predict what happens in people, and the doses used in animal studies don't map neatly onto supplement doses. If you want to cut back on drinking, there are approaches with much better human evidence, including several prescription medicines a doctor can discuss with you. Using St. John's wort for this purpose also brings along all the drug interactions described above.

## St. John's Wort and Hangovers

There is no good evidence that St. John's wort prevents or eases hangovers. No meaningful human research has tested it for this. A few points are worth knowing, though:

- **It won't stop the next-day mood dip.** Some people take it hoping to soften "hangxiety," the anxious, low feeling after a night out. Because the herb's effect (if any) builds over weeks, a dose the morning after won't do much for how you feel that day.
- **It can add to next-day sensitivity.** St. John's wort can make skin more sensitive to sunlight. If you're spending a hungover afternoon outdoors, sunscreen matters more than usual. Extra sun on top of dehydration isn't a great mix.
- **Check what else you take the morning after.** As noted above, cold and cough products with dextromethorphan don't mix well with St. John's wort.

For a hangover headache, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) for the habits with the best evidence. If you're curious about other calming herbs people try around drinking, our guides to [valerian root and alcohol](/never-hungover/valerian-root-and-alcohol) and [kava and alcohol](/never-hungover/kava-and-alcohol) cover their own risks.

## How Long After Stopping St. John's Wort Can You Drink?

There's no special waiting period for alcohol itself, since the herb doesn't strongly affect how your body clears alcohol. The waiting period that matters is for **other medicines**.

Because St. John's wort works by making your body produce more drug-clearing enzymes, its effect doesn't vanish the day you stop. The extra enzymes take time to fade. Drug labels and interaction references commonly advise allowing around two weeks after stopping St. John's wort before relying on medicines it interacts with, and some doctors suggest a similar gap before starting a prescription antidepressant. If you're switching from St. John's wort to a prescription medicine, your doctor should guide the timing.

Stopping suddenly after long-term use can also cause some people to feel dizzy, irritable, or low for a while, similar to stopping some antidepressants. If you've been taking it daily for months, ask about tapering rather than stopping overnight.

## Does St. John's Wort Hurt Your Liver?

St. John's wort isn't generally known as a cause of liver damage. The US National Institutes of Health's LiverTox database describes liver injury from St. John's wort as rare. The more important liver issue is the enzyme effect described above, which isn't damage. It's your liver working harder on other drugs.

Alcohol, on the other hand, is a well-established cause of liver stress when you drink heavily or often. If liver health is part of why you're reading this, the alcohol side of the equation matters far more than the herb. Our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) compares the evidence for common liver-support options.

## Who Should Avoid St. John's Wort Entirely

Talk to your doctor before taking St. John's wort, with or without alcohol, if you:

- Take **any prescription medicine**, especially antidepressants, birth control, blood thinners, heart medicines, HIV drugs, transplant drugs, cancer drugs, or anti-anxiety medicines
- Have **bipolar disorder** or a family history of it
- Are **pregnant or breastfeeding**, since there isn't enough safety data
- Are scheduled for **surgery or anesthesia**, since it can affect anesthesia drugs. Many surgeons ask patients to stop it in advance.
- Have been diagnosed with **moderate to severe depression**, where proven treatments matter
- Drink heavily most days

## When to Get Help Right Away

Most people who have a drink while taking St. John's wort will feel fine. But know these warning signs.

**Signs of serotonin syndrome (get emergency care, call 911 in the US):**

- Agitation, restlessness, or confusion
- Racing heart or high blood pressure
- High fever and heavy sweating
- Muscle twitching, jerking, or stiffness, or overactive reflexes
- Shivering, diarrhea, or dilated pupils

These usually appear within hours of starting or increasing a serotonin-boosting medicine. They can be mistaken for a bad hangover or anxiety, which is why it's worth knowing them in advance.

**Other reasons to call your doctor soon:**

- Your mood is getting worse, or you're drinking more to cope
- Unusual bleeding or bruising if you take a blood thinner
- Breakthrough bleeding while on birth control
- Signs that a regular medicine has stopped working (for example, anxiety or seizure control slipping)

**If you're having thoughts of suicide or self-harm,** call or text 988 in the US, or go to the nearest emergency room. This is not something to wait out.

## A Better Plan for Drinking Nights

If your doctor or pharmacist has said an occasional drink is okay for you, these habits help:

- **Get the okay first.** Ask your doctor or pharmacist whether alcohol is fine with your full medication list, and stay within whatever limit they give you.
- **Eat before and during.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
- **Alternate with water.** Dehydration makes next-day headaches and low mood worse.
- **Skip the medicine-cabinet scramble.** Don't reach for cough or cold products the morning after without checking for dextromethorphan.
- **Notice your mood the next day.** If drinking reliably leaves you lower for a day or two, that's useful information for you and your doctor.

You may see hangover supplements such as DHM (dihydromyricetin) suggested for drinking nights. We don't recommend adding any supplement on top of St. John's wort without a pharmacist's review: lab studies suggest DHM may itself interact with liver enzymes, there's essentially no data on combining it with St. John's wort, and stacking supplements makes the interaction picture harder to read. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains why that check matters. No supplement changes the basic advice above about alcohol and your other medicines.

## The Bottom Line

- St. John's wort and alcohol don't have a well-documented direct reaction, but the herb is a serious interaction risk with many medicines, so ask your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on it.
- The herb doesn't meaningfully change how your body clears alcohol. Its main effect is speeding up the breakdown of many **other** drugs.
- Alcohol works against the mood benefit people take St. John's wort for, and regular drinking can cancel it out.
- The real danger is the three-way mix: St. John's wort, alcohol, and other medicines such as antidepressants, birth control, blood thinners, or anti-anxiety drugs.
- Never combine St. John's wort with prescription antidepressants, triptans, or tramadol on your own, and know the signs of serotonin syndrome.
- If you take any prescription medicine, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using St. John's wort, and tell them how much you drink.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking St. John's wort?**

For a healthy adult who takes no other medicine, an occasional light drink is unlikely to cause a serious problem, and there's no well-documented dangerous chemical reaction between the two. But alcohol can add to dizziness and drowsiness, and regular drinking works against the mood benefit people take the herb for. If you take any prescription medicine, talk to your doctor or pharmacist first, because St. John's wort changes how many drugs work.

**Does St. John's wort make you more drunk?**

There's no good evidence that St. John's wort raises your blood alcohol level or slows how fast you sober up. Alcohol is mostly broken down by enzymes the herb doesn't strongly affect. Some people do feel more dizzy or tired when they combine them, because both can cause those effects, so try one drink first and see how you react.

**Is it dangerous to mix St. John's wort, alcohol, and antidepressants?**

Yes, this combination can be risky. St. John's wort combined with SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, or dextromethorphan can cause serotonin syndrome, a dangerous build-up of serotonin. Alcohol can make the early signs harder to notice and also worsens depression on its own. Don't combine St. John's wort with a prescription antidepressant unless your doctor approves it, and get emergency care for agitation, fever, racing heart, or muscle twitching.

**Does St. John's wort help with alcohol cravings?**

There is no good evidence from human studies that it does. The idea comes from rat studies, where hypericum extracts lowered how much alcohol the animals chose to drink, but that hasn't been shown in people. If you want to cut back on drinking, a doctor can discuss approaches with much better human evidence, including prescription medicines.

**How long after stopping St. John's wort can I drink or start other medicines?**

There's no special wait for alcohol itself. The wait that matters is for other medicines, because St. John's wort's effect on drug-clearing enzymes fades gradually. Interaction references commonly advise allowing around two weeks after stopping before relying on drugs it interacts with. If you're switching to a prescription antidepressant or another medicine, let your doctor set the timing.

**Can St. John's wort and alcohol affect birth control?**

St. John's wort can make hormonal birth control less effective by speeding up how fast your body clears the hormones, and breakthrough bleeding and unplanned pregnancies have been reported. Separately, vomiting after heavy drinking can stop a pill from being absorbed if it happens within a few hours of taking it. If you use hormonal birth control, talk to your prescriber and use a backup method.

**Does St. John's wort help with hangovers?**

There is no good evidence that St. John's wort prevents or eases hangovers, and it hasn't been meaningfully tested for this. Any mood effect it has builds over weeks, so a dose the morning after won't do much. It can also make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. Hydration, food, and drinking less have far better support.

**Is St. John's wort bad for your liver if you drink?**

St. John's wort is rarely linked to liver damage, according to the NIH's LiverTox database. Its main liver effect is speeding up the enzymes that clear other drugs, which isn't damage. Alcohol is the bigger liver concern, especially with heavy or frequent drinking. If you have liver disease, talk to your doctor before taking any supplement.
